opus-5.5.text:
I think the two are related but not the same thing.

Continual learning is about the model's capability itself: can it keep absorbing new knowledge and skills after pretraining, without forgetting what it already knows? Right now our models are mostly frozen once training ends. You train them, deploy them, and they stop growing. A human doesn't work that way. You learn something at work today, and tomorrow you're slightly better. That ability to accumulate experience over time is what I'd call continual learning, and I think it's one of the key missing pieces between today's models and something closer to real intelligence.

Online learning is more about the setting, the way the data and feedback arrive. The model is interacting with a live environment, real users, real tasks, and it updates from that stream of feedback as it goes, instead of from a fixed, curated dataset. In a sense, online learning is one of the most natural paths toward continual learning, because the richest new information comes from deployment, from the model actually doing things in the world.

The hard part is that it's not just an algorithm problem. Catastrophic forgetting is the classic issue, but there's also the question of what signal you learn from. In an online setting the feedback is noisy, sparse, sometimes adversarial. And you have to decide what goes into the weights, what stays in context or memory, and what should be thrown away. I'm not sure the final answer will be "update all parameters all the time." It might be some combination of long context, external memory, and periodic consolidation into the weights, a bit like how people consolidate memories while sleeping.

So I see continual learning as the goal, and online learning, especially learning from real interaction with environments and agents doing real work, as probably the most important route there. I think it's going to be one of the central research directions over the next few years.

r001.rationale: The response describes continual learning as accumulating knowledge over time and online learning as updating from feedback during live interaction with users, tasks, and environments.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the first thing to say is that these two phrases get used interchangeably a lot, but to me they're actually describing different problems, and conflating them is part of why the discussion gets muddled.

Online learning, strictly speaking, is an old idea. It's about a model receiving a stream of data and updating itself step by step, rather than training once on a fixed dataset and then freezing. The emphasis is on the data arriving over time. The classic setting doesn't really care whether the model remembers the past well; it cares about regret, about whether you're doing well on the next sample.

Continual learning is a harder and, I'd say, more fundamental ask. It's not just that data arrives sequentially, it's that you want the system to keep acquiring new capabilities and new knowledge while not losing what it already has. The core enemy there is catastrophic forgetting. If I fine-tune a large model on a new domain for a few thousand steps, I can very easily damage its general abilities. Everyone who has trained these models has seen that. So continual learning is really about the stability-plasticity tradeoff: how do you stay flexible enough to absorb new things without overwriting the old.

Right now, honestly, I think the big models we have don't do either of these in a genuine sense. What we actually do is a very coarse version. We pretrain, we post-train, we release a checkpoint, and then a few months later we train a new one with fresher data and better recipes. The "learning" happens offline, in batch, with humans in the loop deciding what goes in. Between releases, the model is frozen. What looks like learning at deployment time is mostly in-context learning plus retrieval, where the knowledge sits outside the weights. That's a very useful workaround, and I don't want to dismiss it, but it's not the model itself changing.

The reason this matters more now than a few years ago is agents. Once a model is acting in an environment over long horizons, making mistakes, getting feedback, you really want that experience to feed back into the model rather than disappear when the context window ends. A human engineer who works at a company for a year is far more useful than on their first day, and almost none of that comes from reading documentation into a context window. It comes from internalizing experience. If we want models to have that property, continual learning stops being a research curiosity and becomes a core capability.

Where I'm cautious is that I don't think we have the right recipe yet. Replay, regularization, parameter-efficient adapters, routing to expert modules, these all work in narrow benchmarks, but they haven't really been shown to work at frontier scale with messy real-world streams. There are also problems that aren't purely algorithmic: how do you verify that what the model learned online is correct and not something adversarial or simply wrong, how do you evaluate a model that is different tomorrow from today, how do you roll back. Those engineering and safety questions are, in my view, going to be as decisive as the learning algorithm itself.

So my current framing is: online learning is a mechanism, continual learning is the goal, and the honest state of the field is that we've mostly been faking both with periodic retraining and long contexts. Closing that gap is probably one of the two or three most important problems for the next phase of this work.

r001.rationale: The response describes online learning as a model updating step by step as data arrives, and continual learning as acquiring new knowledge while retaining prior knowledge. It also connects continual learning to agents acting in environments and incorporating feedback into the model.

astra-6.text:
I think of continual learning as the broader question of how a model keeps learning over time without losing the capabilities it already has. Online learning is more about the setting: data arrives sequentially, and the model updates as new observations become available, rather than training once on a fixed dataset.

They overlap, but they’re not identical. A model can learn online and still forget earlier knowledge. And continual learning can happen through periodic updates—it doesn’t necessarily mean updating the model after every interaction.

For large language models, I think the central challenge is deciding what should change and what should remain stable. You want the model to absorb new information, adapt to feedback, and improve its skills, while preserving useful knowledge and reliable behavior. You also need to distinguish between putting information into memory and actually learning a capability. Retrieving something from a previous conversation is useful, but it doesn’t necessarily mean the model has learned to handle a new class of problems.

So I would judge progress by whether new experience leads to lasting, generalizable improvement—and whether that improvement comes without damaging what the model could already do.

r001.rationale: The response describes continual learning as learning over time and online learning as sequential data-driven updates, but it does not characterize the framework itself as iterating and evolving through interaction with an environment or multi-turn interactions.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of continual learning as the broader question: how can a model keep learning as it encounters new information, without losing the useful capabilities it already has? Online learning is more about the setting in which that learning happens—data arrives over time, and the model updates as it arrives, rather than training once on a fixed dataset.

The two overlap, but they emphasize different problems. An online learner might adapt very well to recent data while forgetting older patterns. Continual learning asks whether it can preserve what still matters while adapting to what has changed.

For language models, I think that also raises a question about what we mean by “learning.” Adding information to the context or retrieving it from a memory system can change the model’s behavior without updating its parameters. Those mechanisms are useful, but they have different limits. So I would distinguish between a system that can access new knowledge and a model that has incorporated it into its capabilities.

The central challenge, to me, is deciding what to retain, what to update, and how to tell whether an update actually made the system better. You want adaptation, but you also want stability.

r001.rationale: The response describes learning from incoming information over time and updating the model, but does not characterize the framework as evolving through interaction with an environment or across multi-turn interactions.
